## {}

<!-- 
Why ensembling is good

- averaging model uncertainty -- Uncertainty over which model is closest to the data generating process is averaged over.
- more robust
- better calibrated forecasts (uncertainty)
- ...

Downsides

- more complex
- more computationally expensive
-->

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Why use ensemble forecasts?

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## ✅ Advantages

The fundamental benefit of ensembling is that it **averages over model uncertainty**. This produces forecasts that are:

- *More accurate*: generally better than any single model
- *More robust*: less sensitive to any single model
- *Better calibrated*: forecast uncertainty incorporates uncertainty of model specification.
:::
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## ⚠️ Downsides

- *More complex*: to specify, tune, and interpret
- *More expensive*: many models to fit and forecast
:::
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/andrik-langfield-0rTCXZM7Xfo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}


## {}

<!-- 
Three ways to average forecasts
-->

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Three ways to average forecasts

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## 🎲 Mean of random variables

$$\bar{X} = \sum_{i} w_i X_i$$

Averaging **outcomes** (samples)
:::
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔀 Probability Mixture (linear pooling)

$$ F(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot F_i(x), \hspace{1em} f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot f_i(x) $$

Averaging **probabilities** (PDF/CDF)
:::
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## 📊 Quantile Mixture (Vincentization)

$$ F^{-1}(p) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot F_i^{-1}(p) $$

Averaging **quantiles** (inverse CDF)
:::
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/andrik-langfield-0rTCXZM7Xfo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

<!-- 
## {}

Three ways to average forecasts

: callout
Mean of random variables
Xˉ=i∑​wiXi​

    combines actual random quantities
    distribution depends on dependence/covariance

: callout
Probability Mixture (linear pooling)

$$ F(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot F_i(x), \hspace{1em} f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot f_i(x) $$

    averages probabilities directly
    preserves multimodality
    easy to compute

: callout
Quantile Mixture (Vincentization)

$$ F^{-1}(p) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot F_i^{-1}(p) $$

    averages outcome levels at each probability
    often used for forecast combination
    generally different from the mixture

![](../backgrounds/andrik-langfield-0rTCXZM7Xfo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}
-->

## {}

<!-- 
### Ensemble weights $w_i$

Note: inverse variance weighting is the optimal choice for minimising the variance of
the combined point forecast when model errors are uncorrelated. When errors are
correlated, the optimal weights require the full error covariance matrix — an analogy
to the OLS vs MinT distinction in reconciliation.
-->

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Ensemble weights $w_i$

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## ⚖️ Equal weighting

$$w_i = 1/N$$

Default; robust when model ranking is uncertain.
:::
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## 📉 Performance-based weighting

$$w_i \propto 1/\hat\sigma^2_i \quad \text{or} \quad w_i \propto 1/\widehat{\text{MSE}}_i$$

Weight by inverse variance or inverse MSE.
:::
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## 🗺️ Feature-based weighting

$$w_i = f(\text{series features})$$

FFORMS selects a single model ($w_i \in \{0,1\}$);  
FFORMA estimates weights from series features ($w_i \in [0,1]$).
:::
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/elena-mozhvilo-j06gLuKK0GM-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

<!-- Other weighting strategies not shown:
  - Bayesian model averaging (BMA): weights as posterior model probabilities given data
  - Regime-switching weights: weights change depending on detected state (e.g. expansion vs recession)
  - Online learning / aggregation of experts: weights updated sequentially as new data arrives (e.g. exponential weighting)
-->

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Other weighting strategies

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## ⏳ Time-varying weights

Some models are better short-term, others long-term.
:::
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔄 Online / adaptive weights

Weights updated iteratively as new observations arrive.
:::
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## 🧑‍💼 Expert judgement

Weights reflect model credibility rather than past performance alone.
:::
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/elena-mozhvilo-j06gLuKK0GM-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

::: columns

:::

### Australian ambulance costs

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| label: ambulance_data
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
library(fable)
library(tsibble)
library(ggplot2)
ambulance <- tsibble(
  Year = 2005:2024, 
  Revenue = c(2.25, 2.38, 2.47, 2.67, 2.9, 2.99, 3.09, 
              3.25, 3.45, 3.48, 3.44, 3.66, 3.96, 4.26,
              4.46, 4.64, 5, 5.29, 5.74, 5.64),
  index = Year
)
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: ambulance_plot
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 7
ambulance |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Year, y = Revenue)) + 
  geom_line()
```

:::{.fragment .fade-up fragment-index=1}

:::{.callout-caution}
## Future trend?

The trend changed in 2015 after a drop.

Will it change again following the 2024 drop?
:::

:::

:::
:::

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

### Australian ambulance costs

```{r}
#| label: ambulance_forecast
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 7
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
ambulance_fc <- ambulance |>
  model(
    ETS = ETS(Revenue),
    `TSLM Piecewise` = TSLM(Revenue ~ trend(knots = 2015))
  ) |>
  mutate(
    `Mean of RV` = (ETS + `TSLM Piecewise`)/2L
  ) |> 
  forecast(h = "10 years")
avg_ensemble <- ambulance_fc |>
  filter(.model == "Mean of RV")
ambulance_fc <- ambulance_fc |>
  filter(.model != "Mean of RV")
ambulance_fc |>
  autoplot(ambulance) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/mpho-mojapelo-s6Vv9u2qZyc-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}

## {}

<!-- 
Three ways to average forecasts
-->

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Three ways to average forecasts

:::{.callout-note icon=false}
## 🎲 Mean of random variables (averaging outcomes)

```r
combination_ensemble(ETS, ARIMA) # OR (ETS + ARIMA)/2L
```

$$\bar{X} = \sum_{i} w_i X_i$$

:::

::: blur
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔀 Probability Mixture (averaging probabilities)

```r
dist_mixture(fc1, fc2, type = "probability", weights = c(0.5, 0.5))
```

$$ F(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot F_i(x), \hspace{1em} f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot f_i(x) $$
:::
:::

::: blur
:::{.callout-warning icon=false}
## 📊 Quantile Mixture (averaging quantiles)

```r
dist_mixture(fc1, fc2, type = "quantile", weights = c(0.5, 0.5))
```

$$ F^{-1}(p) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot F_i^{-1}(p) $$

:::
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/andrik-langfield-0rTCXZM7Xfo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Probability mixtures

```{r}
#| label: prob_mixture_cdf
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 7
prob_ensemble <- fc_2030 |>
  group_by(Year) |> 
  summarise(
    .model = "Probability Mixture",
    Revenue = `dimnames<-`(do.call(dist_mixture, c(as.list(Revenue), weights = list(c(0.5, 0.5)), type = "probability")), "Revenue")
  )

prob_ensemble |> 
  bind_rows(fc_2030) |> 
  rowwise() |> 
  reframe(.model, x = seq(5, 8.3, by = 0.01), cdf = cdf(Revenue, x)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(colour = .model, x = x, y = cdf)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  labs(x = "Revenue", y = "Probability", title = "Forecasts of ambulance costs in 2030") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") + 
  annotate("segment", x = 7.2, xend = 7.2, y = 0, yend = 1, linetype = "dashed") + 
  geom_segment(aes(y = cdf(Revenue, 7.2), yend = cdf(Revenue, 7.2)), x = 0, xend = 7.2, linetype = "dashed", data = bind_rows(prob_ensemble, fc_2030))
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/andrik-langfield-0rTCXZM7Xfo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

### Exercise: Ensemble forecasting

Produce an ensemble for Australian Electricity Production (`aus_production`).

1. Fit several models for electricity production

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| label: exercise-fit
fit <- aus_production |>
  model(
    ETS   = ETS(Electricity),
    ARIMA = ARIMA(sqrt(Electricity))
  )
fit
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/randy-fath-R5_1N6ZgCOo-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}

## {}

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Exercise: Ensemble forecasting

2. Combine them into an equal-weighted ensemble

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| label: exercise-ensemble
fit_ensemble <- fit |>
  mutate(
    Ensemble = combination_ensemble(ETS, ARIMA)
    # Ensemble = (ETS + ARIMA) / 2L
  )
fit_ensemble |>
  forecast(h = "2 years") |>
  autoplot(tail(aus_production, 20), alpha = 0.3)
```

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/randy-fath-R5_1N6ZgCOo-unsplash.jpg){.image-left}

### Exercise: Ensemble forecasting

   Can you beat equal weighting?

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| label: exercise-weights
fit_ensemble |>
  mutate(
    W_Ensemble = combination_ensemble(ETS, ARIMA, weights = "inv_var")
  ) |>
  accuracy() |>
  arrange(RMSE)
```

### Exercise: Ensemble forecasting

4. Experiment with unequal weights  
   Can you beat equal weighting?

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| label: exercise-weights-cv
aus_production |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 40, .step = 4) |>
  model(
    ETS   = ETS(Electricity),
    ARIMA = ARIMA(sqrt(Electricity))
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Ensemble   = combination_ensemble(ETS, ARIMA),
    W_Ensemble = combination_ensemble(ETS, ARIMA, weights = "inv_var")
  ) |>
  forecast(h = 4) |>
  accuracy(aus_production) |>
  arrange(RMSE)
```

In-sample accuracy is unrealistic for actual forecasting performance.

## {}

<!-- 
- The **forecast combination puzzle** is the recurring empirical pattern that optimally weighted combinations often do not beat simple equal-weighted averages, even when the component models differ in quality.
 
  - Frazier, Covey, Martin & Poskitt (2023, arXiv:2308.05263) argue that much of the puzzle comes from the usual **two-step** workflow: estimate the component models first, then estimate the combination weights.
  
  - In this setting, standard predictive-accuracy tests can have a **nonstandard asymptotic null distribution**, which leads to size distortions and low power.
  
  - Their proposed fix is to estimate the component-model parameters and combination weights **jointly in one step, when feasible**. Under that approach, the puzzle largely disappears and the optimally estimated combination can show its advantage when it is genuinely better.
-->

<!-- nonstandard asymptotic null distribution → size distortions and low power in predictive-accuracy tests -->

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Forecast combination puzzle

Finding ensemble weights that outperform equal weights is surprisingly difficult.

(Even when models clearly differ in quality.)

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## ✅ Solving the puzzle

Frazier, Covey, Martin & Poskitt (2023) solve the puzzle and explain the root cause.
:::
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/nathalia-segato-V9qc-JVKIBo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}


::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Forecast combination puzzle

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🪜 The two-step workflow

1. Estimate component models
2. Estimate combination weights

Each step ignores uncertainty from the other.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Frazier, Covey, Martin & Poskitt (2023) explore jointly estimating models with weights.
:::

:::{.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔗 Joint estimation

Estimate model parameters and weights together:

$$(\hat\theta, \hat w) = \arg\min_{\theta,\, w} \mathcal{L}(y, \textstyle\sum_i w_i f_i(\theta_i))$$

Joint estimation produces better results with unequal weights.
:::
:::

:::
:::

![](../backgrounds/nathalia-segato-V9qc-JVKIBo-unsplash.jpg){.image-right}

## {}

<!-- 
Aside: Large forecasting models

Synthetic data is widely used in training foundation models for forecasting.

Simulating data from weighted ensembles allows learning of more generalised patterns, essentially training large models to learn solutions to the forecast combination problem.
-->

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

### Aside: Synthetic data for LFMs

Weighted ensembles are used to simulate synthetic time series for training large forecasting models (LFMs).

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🎲 Simulating from an ensemble

Generate diverse synthetic time series with different weighted combinations of component model simulations.

:::
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
:::{.callout-tip icon=false}
## 📐 Why this is useful

- Foundation models learn unequal weights of models
- Essentially learns combinations without the puzzle
- Covers a wider range of temporal structures
:::
:::
